papers.title: Textless Speech-to-Speech Translation from Nepali to English Using Discrete Units: A Deep Learning Approach
papers.abstract: This study implements direct speech to speech translation eliminating the conventional need for Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Machine Translation (MT) by leveraging HuBERT for discrete unit extraction, a Transformer-based encoder-decoder for translation, and HiFi-GAN for speech reconstruction. Inspired by recent advances in unit-based S2ST, the model is trained on the multilingual FLEURS dataset for Nepali to English language translation. It achieved a BLEU score of 42.80, demonstrating both translation accuracy and natural-sounding speech synthesis. This work offers a scalable and effective solution for low-resource languages like Nepali.

papers.title: Multi-Task Flow Matching Speech Enhancement Method with Dual Guidance of Semantic Understanding and Speaker Perception
papers.abstract: Generative speech enhancement models often suffer from the “generative hallucination” issue, where artifacts are introduced or original speech characteristics are distorted during reconstruction due to insufficient prior constraints, severely limiting their practicality. To address this, we propose a multi-task flow-matching speech enhancement network with dual guidance from semantic understanding and speaker perception. The method employs a flow-matching model as the generative backbone, leveraging both semantic and speaker embeddings as auxiliary conditions to guide the denoising process. The semantic embedding, extracted by a pretrained audio foundation model, provides high-level content priors to ensure the intelligibility and clarity of the enhanced speech. The speaker embedding, derived from a speaker verification model, captures timbre representations, which are further regularized by a contrastive InfoNCE loss to enhance intra-class compactness and inter-class separability of speaker characteristics. During optimization, the primary denoising reconstruction task and the auxiliary speaker discrimination task are jointly optimized. The two guidance streams, together with acoustic features, are collaboratively fed into the generation network, effectively suppressing hallucinations from both content correctness and timbre consistency perspectives. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed multi-task framework substantially mitigates hallucination-related errors in generative scenarios, achieving comprehensive improvements in objective metrics, including both reference-based measures and non-intrusive perceptual metrics, thus validating the effectiveness of the dual-guidance strategy for generative speech enhancement.

# OpenVoice V2 ONNX Models

This repository provides the speaker encoder and tone color converter from
**OpenVoice V2** in ONNX format for local voice cloning and voice conversion.
The models can run through **ONNX Runtime** in C#, C++, Python, Rust, and other
supported environments without a PyTorch runtime.

The original architecture and model weights were developed by **MyShell and
the OpenVoice contributors**. See the [upstream OpenVoice project](https://github.com/myshell-ai/OpenVoice).

The converter takes speech audio and changes its voice characteristics using
source and target speaker embeddings. A separate text-to-speech system supplies
the base speech when generating audio from text.

## 📦 Repository Contents

| File | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `tone_extract.onnx` | Extracts a 256-dimensional speaker embedding from a reference spectrogram. |
| `tone_color.onnx` | Converts a source spectrogram using source and target speaker embeddings. |
| `tone_config.json` | Audio preprocessing parameters and OpenVoice V2 network configuration. |
| `LICENSE` | Original MIT license and copyright notice. |

Download files using:

```text
https://huggingface.co/Hinotsuba/OpenVoice-ONNX-v2/resolve/main/{filename}
```

Use a specific repository revision in place of `main` when pinning a deployment.

## 🛠️ Tensor Specifications

All floating-point tensors use **float32**. Both graphs have a fixed batch size
of **1**. `frames` denotes the number of spectrogram frames, not waveform samples.

### Speaker Encoder: `tone_extract.onnx`

| Direction | Name | Type | Shape | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Input | `input` | float32 | `[1, frames, 513]` | Reference audio magnitude spectrogram, with time before frequency. |
| Output | `tone_embedding` | float32 | `[1, 256]` | Speaker embedding. |

Reshape the extracted embedding to `[1, 256, 1]` before passing it to the converter.

### Tone Color Converter: `tone_color.onnx`

| Direction | Name | Type | Shape | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Input | `audio` | float32 | `[1, 513, frames]` | Source audio magnitude spectrogram, with frequency before time. |
| Input | `audio_length` | int64 | `[1]` | Number of source spectrogram frames. |
| Input | `src_tone` | float32 | `[1, 256, 1]` | Embedding of the source or base voice. |
| Input | `dest_tone` | float32 | `[1, 256, 1]` | Embedding of the target voice. |
| Input | `tau` | float32 | `[1]` | Explicit latent perturbation scale. |
| Output | `converted_audio` | float32 | `[1, 1, length]` | Mono waveform at 22050 Hz; the first two axes are batch and channel. |

For a single unpadded input, set `audio_length[0]` to `frames`. Read
`converted_audio[0, 0, :]` to obtain the one-dimensional waveform. These samples
are audio data; encoding them as WAV or another format is the caller's responsibility.

## Audio Preparation

Prepare the spectrogram outside the ONNX graphs. The same preprocessing applies
to reference audio and source audio; only the tensor axis order differs.

Decode and resample to **mono float PCM at 22050 Hz**, using the conventional
PCM amplitude scale of approximately `[-1, 1]`. Then match the upstream
[`spectrogram_torch` implementation](https://github.com/myshell-ai/OpenVoice/blob/main/openvoice/mel_processing.py):

| Parameter | Value |
| --- | --- |
| FFT size (`n_fft` / `filter_length`) | `1024` |
| Hop length | `256` |
| Window length | `1024` |
| Window | Periodic Hann |
| Padding before STFT | Reflect padding, `384` samples on each side |
| STFT centering | `false` |
| FFT normalization | `false` |
| Frequency bins | One-sided, `513` bins |
| Spectrum values | Linear magnitude: `sqrt(real * real + imag * imag + 1e-6)` |

Use a library with these settings or reproduce the same window, padding, FFT
scaling, and magnitude calculation. The graphs expect this linear spectrum,
with no mel projection or logarithmic scaling.

## 🚀 Inference Workflow

1. Obtain clean reference speech from the source voice and the target speaker.
   For a TTS source, use a reference clip from the same base voice that will
   generate the speech.
2. Prepare each reference spectrogram and run `tone_extract.onnx`. Reshape the
   results to `[1, 256, 1]` for `src_tone` and `dest_tone`.
3. Generate or load the source speech. Prepare its spectrogram as `[1, 513, frames]`.
4. Run `tone_color.onnx` with the source spectrogram, its frame count, both
   embeddings, and an explicit `tau` value.
5. Read the mono waveform from `converted_audio` and encode or play it at
   `22050 Hz`. Resample separately if the output device needs another rate.

These models are used by [Tsubaki TTS Engine](https://github.com/MrHryhorii/SmartStack/tree/main/ONNX_Runner)
for local C#/.NET text-to-speech with Piper synthesis, OpenVoice V2 voice
cloning, and audio streaming without a Python runtime.

## Export Behavior and Limits

### Temperature: `tau`

`tau` is a required ONNX input and has no automatic default. In the upstream
Python implementation, the internal `voice_conversion()` method defaults to
`1.0`, while the public [`ToneColorConverter.convert()` method](https://github.com/myshell-ai/OpenVoice/blob/main/openvoice/api.py)
defaults to `0.3`.

This export contains a **fixed noise tensor**. `tau` scales the latent
perturbation drawn from that tensor: lower values reduce the perturbation, and
`0` removes its contribution. Repeated CPU calls with identical inputs and
`tau` values produced identical output in verification. Fresh noise is not
sampled on each call.

### Input Length

The converter's fixed noise tensor has shape `[1, 192, 32768]`, limiting a single
conversion to **32768 spectrogram frames** despite the dynamic time axis.
At a hop length of `256` and output rate of `22050 Hz`, this corresponds to
approximately **380 seconds of output audio**. Split longer audio into shorter
chunks before conversion.

### Runtime and Export Metadata

| Model | ONNX opset | ONNX IR version | Export producer metadata |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `tone_extract.onnx` | `11` | `6` | PyTorch `2.1.2` |
| `tone_color.onnx` | `17` | `8` | PyTorch `2.1.2` |

CPU inference was verified with **ONNX Runtime 1.29.0**, including dynamic frame
counts and explicit `tau` values. Execution-provider support and performance
depend on the runtime, hardware, and application.

The export script and exact upstream checkpoint revision are not included in
this package. The metadata above describes the distributed ONNX files.

# Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507: transcribe.cpp GGUF

GGUF conversions of [mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507](https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507) for use
with [transcribe.cpp](https://github.com/handy-computer/transcribe.cpp).

Ported from upstream commit
[3060fe3](https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507/commit/3060fe3),
pinned 2026-06-06.
Validated against the Transformers reference at transcribe.cpp commit
[483c122](https://github.com/handy-computer/transcribe.cpp/tree/483c122)
on 2026-06-06.

Offline audio-LLM speech-to-text and speech translation. A Whisper-large-v3
bidirectional audio encoder feeds a 4-frame-group projector (375 audio tokens
per 30 s chunk) into a Ministral-3B causal LM (30 layers, GQA 32/8, NEOX RoPE,
SwiGLU) via audio-token injection. Takes a 16 kHz mono WAV and produces a
transcript via greedy decoding; speech translation runs through the
mistral-common instruct template. The smaller sibling of Voxtral Small 24B —
same encoder, projector, log-mel frontend, and tekken tokenizer, with a 3B
decoder in place of Mistral-Small-24B.

# Voxtral Mini 1.0 (3B) - 2507

Voxtral Mini is an enhancement of [Ministral 3B](https://mistral.ai/news/ministraux), incorporating state-of-the-art audio input capabilities while retaining best-in-class text performance. It excels at speech transcription, translation and audio understanding.

Learn more about Voxtral in our blog post [here](https://mistral.ai/news/voxtral) and our [research paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13264).

## Key Features

Voxtral builds upon Ministral-3B with powerful audio understanding capabilities.
- **Dedicated transcription mode**: Voxtral can operate in a pure speech transcription mode to maximize performance. By default, Voxtral automatically predicts the source audio language and transcribes the text accordingly
- **Long-form context**: With a 32k token context length, Voxtral handles audios up to 30 minutes for transcription, or 40 minutes for understanding
- **Built-in Q&A and summarization**: Supports asking questions directly through audio. Analyze audio and generate structured summaries without the need for separate ASR and language models
- **Natively multilingual**: Automatic language detection and state-of-the-art performance in the world’s most widely used languages (English, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Hindi, German, Dutch, Italian)
- **Function-calling straight from voice**: Enables direct triggering of backend functions, workflows, or API calls based on spoken user intents
- **Highly capable at text**: Retains the text understanding capabilities of its language model backbone, Ministral-3B

### vLLM (recommended)

We recommend using this model with [vLLM](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm).

#### Installation

Make sure to install vllm >= 0.10.0, we recommend using `uv`:

```
uv pip install -U "vllm[audio]" --system
```

Doing so should automatically install [`mistral_common >= 1.8.1`](https://github.com/mistralai/mistral-common/releases/tag/v1.8.1).

To check:
```
python -c "import mistral_common; print(mistral_common.__version__)"
```

#### Offline

You can test that your vLLM setup works as expected by cloning the vLLM repo:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm && cd vllm
```

and then running:

```sh
python examples/offline_inference/audio_language.py --num-audios 2 --model-type voxtral
```

#### Serve

We recommend that you use Voxtral-Small-24B-2507 in a server/client setting. 

1. Spin up a server:

```
vllm serve mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507 --tokenizer_mode mistral --config_format mistral --load_format mistral
```

**Note:** Running Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507 on GPU requires ~9.5 GB of GPU RAM in bf16 or fp16. 


2. To ping the client you can use a simple Python snippet. See the following examples.


### Audio Instruct

Leverage the audio capabilities of Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507 to chat.

Make sure that your client has `mistral-common` with audio installed:

```sh
pip install --upgrade mistral_common\[audio\]
```

```py
from mistral_common.protocol.instruct.messages import TextChunk, AudioChunk, UserMessage, AssistantMessage, RawAudio
from mistral_common.audio import Audio
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download

from openai import OpenAI

# Modify OpenAI's API key and API base to use vLLM's API server.
openai_api_key = "EMPTY"
openai_api_base = "http://<your-server-host>:8000/v1"

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=openai_api_key,
    base_url=openai_api_base,
)

models = client.models.list()
model = models.data[0].id

obama_file = hf_hub_download("patrickvonplaten/audio_samples", "obama.mp3", repo_type="dataset")
bcn_file = hf_hub_download("patrickvonplaten/audio_samples", "bcn_weather.mp3", repo_type="dataset")

def file_to_chunk(file: str) -> AudioChunk:
    audio = Audio.from_file(file, strict=False)
    return AudioChunk.from_audio(audio)

text_chunk = TextChunk(text="Which speaker is more inspiring? Why? How are they different from each other?")
user_msg = UserMessage(content=[file_to_chunk(obama_file), file_to_chunk(bcn_file), text_chunk]).to_openai()

print(30 * "=" + "USER 1" + 30 * "=")
print(text_chunk.text)
print("\n\n")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=model,
    messages=[user_msg],
    temperature=0.2,
    top_p=0.95,
)
content = response.choices[0].message.content

print(30 * "=" + "BOT 1" + 30 * "=")
print(content)
print("\n\n")
# The speaker who is more inspiring is the one who delivered the farewell address, as they express
# gratitude, optimism, and a strong commitment to the nation and its citizens. They emphasize the importance of
# self-government and active citizenship, encouraging everyone to participate in the democratic process. In contrast,
# the other speaker provides a factual update on the weather in Barcelona, which is less inspiring as it
# lacks the emotional and motivational content of the farewell address.

# **Differences:**
# - The farewell address speaker focuses on the values and responsibilities of citizenship, encouraging active participation in democracy.
# - The weather update speaker provides factual information about the temperature in Barcelona, without any emotional or motivational content.


messages = [
    user_msg,
    AssistantMessage(content=content).to_openai(),
    UserMessage(content="Ok, now please summarize the content of the first audio.").to_openai()
]
print(30 * "=" + "USER 2" + 30 * "=")
print(messages[-1]["content"])
print("\n\n")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=model,
    messages=messages,
    temperature=0.2,
    top_p=0.95,
)
content = response.choices[0].message.content
print(30 * "=" + "BOT 2" + 30 * "=")
print(content)
```

**Natiq-dz-ARG** is a production-grade speech synthesis and zero-shot voice cloning model tailored specifically for **Algerian Darija (الدارجة الجزائرية)** with natural French code-switching. It is built as a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) adapter on top of [bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b](https://huggingface.co/bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b).

The model synthesizes high-fidelity **24,000 Hz (24 kHz Mono)** speech conditioned on target text and a short reference audio prompt.

---


## Inference Guidelines & Reference Audio

The model uses zero-shot acoustic conditioning to replicate vocal timbre, cadence, and acoustic environment:

1. **Reference Audio**: Provide a clean, single-speaker audio recording between **2 and 20 seconds**. The audio can be in WAV, MP3, or FLAC format (automatically converted to 24 kHz mono).
2. **Reference Transcript**: Providing an accurate verbatim transcript of what is spoken in the reference audio significantly improves synthesis fidelity and pronunciation.
3. **Target Text**: Enter the text you wish to synthesize in Algerian Darija (Arabic script, Latin transliteration, or natural French code-switching).
4. **Precision**: The model supports `bfloat16` on modern GPUs (Ampere / Ada / Hopper) and `float16` on NVIDIA T4 GPUs.

You can run the model on any CUDA GPU (≥16 GB VRAM) with `transformers` and `peft`. The model architecture code ships in this repo under `model/`:

```python
sys.path.insert(0, repo)
from model.modeling import HiggsMultimodalQwen3ForConditionalGeneration

dtype = torch.bfloat16 if torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported() else torch.float16
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b")
base = HiggsMultimodalQwen3ForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained("bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b", torch_dtype=dtype)
base.prepare_inputs_for_generation = lambda *a, **k: {}  # PEFT compatibility shim
model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base, repo).to("cuda").eval().base_model.model
model.audio_head.weight = model.audio_embedding.weight  # tied weights

ref, sr = sf.read(f"{repo}/sample_voices/ref_tech_developer.wav", dtype="float32")
with torch.inference_mode():
    wav = model.generate_speech(
        "واش راك خويا، واش راهم الدار؟",
        tokenizer,
        reference_audio=torch.from_numpy(ref).unsqueeze(0),
        reference_sample_rate=sr,
        reference_text="Développeur؟ لا لا لا، physicien de base، كيما كان يقول واحد le prof تاع physique، qui peut le plus peut le moins، بلا ما نعايروا حتى واحد.",
        temperature=0.7, top_p=0.95, max_new_tokens=768,
    )
sf.write("natiq_output.wav", wav.float().cpu().numpy().squeeze(), 24000)
```

# MegaTTS3 for TurboSpark

This is ByteDance's MegaTTS3 zero-shot voice cloning model, converted to safetensors
so [TurboSpark](https://github.com/whit3rabbit/turbospark) can install it and run it locally. Give it 1 to 30
seconds of someone's voice and some English text, and it speaks the text in that voice
at 24 kHz. The weights are the upstream values in a new file format, not a retrain or a
fine-tune.

If you are not using TurboSpark, you probably want the
[upstream release](https://huggingface.co/ByteDance/MegaTTS3) instead. These files are
not an MLX model and will not load in mlx-audio, which has no MegaTTS3 port. The
upstream PyTorch code cannot load them either without reversing the conversion.

## Why this exists

TurboSpark is a hobby project: a native macOS app and Rust workspace for running local
models on Apple Silicon. Its runtime reads safetensors only, and its model catalog
installs only files pinned to a commit and a sha256. MegaTTS3 ships as PyTorch pickle
checkpoints, which TurboSpark will not load, because opening a pickle can run code.

Converting once and publishing the result lets the app install MegaTTS3 like any other
model and check every byte before it runs. It also means you can rerun the converter
and compare hashes rather than trusting this upload.

## What is in the repo

| Path | What it is | Params | Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| `config.json` | Root config. TurboSpark dispatches on `model_type: megatts3`, and `voice_clone` says whether the WavVAE encoder is present. |  | 133 B |
| `aligner_lm/` | Whisper-style aligner. Finds the phones and their timing in the reference recording. | 54.6M | 218 MB |
| `duration_lm/` | Duration model. Predicts how long each phone of the new text lasts. | 67.0M | 268 MB |
| `diffusion_transformer/` | 24-layer latent diffusion transformer. Generates the speech latents in the reference voice. | 459.0M | 1.84 GB |
| `wavvae/` | WavVAE codec. The encoder turns the reference into a latent, and the decoder turns latents into 24 kHz audio. | 255.6M | 1.02 GB |
| `g2p/` | Qwen2-0.5B grapheme-to-phoneme model and tokenizer, copied unchanged (bf16). |  | 1.04 GB |
| `frontend/dict.json` | Upstream phone and tone dictionary. Kept for reference, TurboSpark does not read it. |  | 1.75 KB |
| `manifest.json` | sha256, size, and tensor count of every file, plus the upstream sources. |  |  |
| `NOTICE.md` | Exact upstream sources, their sha256, and where the encoder came from. |  | 1.63 KB |
| `LICENSE` | Apache-2.0, from the upstream MegaTTS3 code. |  | 11.3 KB |

Each component folder also has a `config.json` with the upstream hyperparameters and the
sha256 of the checkpoint it came from.

## How it was converted

Every file here comes from `crates/audio/tools/convert_megatts3.py` in the TurboSpark repo.

- It checks each upstream file against a pinned sha256 before reading it.
- It parses the checkpoints with an allowlisted unpickler and never imports torch.
- It widens f16 and bf16 tensors to f32, which loses nothing.
- It stores conv weights as `[out, kernel, in]`, the layout MLX uses, and keeps weight
  norm as separate `weight_g` and `weight_v` tensors.
- It writes the same bytes for the same inputs, so `manifest.json` doubles as a
  reproducibility check.

Sources, also listed with their hashes in `NOTICE.md`:

- [ByteDance/MegaTTS3](https://huggingface.co/ByteDance/MegaTTS3/tree/409a7002b006d80f0730fca6f80441b08c10e738) at `409a7002`: the aligner, duration model, diffusion transformer, and G2P.
- [mrfakename/MegaTTS3-VoiceCloning](https://huggingface.co/mrfakename/MegaTTS3-VoiceCloning/tree/b3a2c297eea319931ee985751f117f866085d0c5) at `b3a2c297`: the WavVAE with its encoder.

## Using it with TurboSpark

Voice cloning is on TurboSpark's `main` branch and not in a release yet. Every entry
point asks you to confirm that you have the right to use the voice.

- **App.** In Audio Studio, open Voice Clone, pick MegaTTS3, accept the download notice,
  and choose or record a reference.
- **Command line.** `turbospark-clone` takes this folder or the installed alias:

```sh
hf download cowWhySo/MegaTTS3-TurboSpark --local-dir MegaTTS3-TurboSpark
turbospark-clone speak --model MegaTTS3-TurboSpark --reference me.wav \
  --text "Hello there." --consent --output hello.wav
```

- **HTTP.** `turbospark-server --tts-model` serves it on the OpenAI-style speech route,
  with the reference as a base64 WAV:

```sh
turbospark-server --tts-model MegaTTS3-TurboSpark
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/audio/speech -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"model\":\"MegaTTS3-TurboSpark\",\"input\":\"Hello there.\",\"consent\":true,\"reference_audio\":\"$(base64 -i me.wav)\"}" \
  -o hello.wav
```

Optional settings are `steps` (default 32, fewer is faster), `p_w` (intelligibility,
default 1.4), `t_w` (similarity to the reference, default 3.0), `seed`, and `speed`.

## Consent and the encoder

ByteDance withheld the WavVAE encoder, the part that turns a recording into a voice the
model can imitate, over misuse concerns. The encoder here is a third-party re-upload by
mrfakename, credited to ModelScope ACoderPassBy/MegaTTS-SFT. Its origin and license were
not independently verified, and the re-upload's repository declares Apache-2.0.

TurboSpark asks you to accept that before it downloads these files, and asks on every
request whether you have the right to use the voice. Please only clone your own voice or
the voice of someone who agreed to it.

## Limits

- English only. TurboSpark's text normalizer covers a documented subset of upstream's, and
  non-Latin text is refused.
- The reference can be 1 to 30 seconds, and only the first 28 are used. Shorter
  references synthesize faster.
- Output is mono 24 kHz.
- It is not fast. On an M4 Max, one reading each, a 3 second sentence at 8 steps took
  35 s on the CPU and about 10 s on TurboSpark's experimental Metal path. The examples
  above use the default 32 steps, four times the diffusion work, so expect them to take
  several times longer. Lower `steps` trades quality for speed.
- TurboSpark's port tracks the PyTorch reference on these weights to within about 1e-3
  per sample. Nobody has run a listening test or a speaker-similarity study on it yet.

The measurements behind these numbers are in the [port's README](https://github.com/whit3rabbit/turbospark/blob/main/crates/audio/src/tts/megatts3/README.md).

[weights](https://huggingface.co/ByteDance/MegaTTS3). Thanks to them for releasing it
under Apache-2.0, and to mrfakename for the encoder re-upload.

# VoxCPM2 — prebuilt weight sets for PyTorch

[VoxCPM2](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/VoxCPM2) prebuilt for the PyTorch engine of
[Voicebox-on-Linux](https://github.com/grruwi/Voicebox-on-Linux), cut exactly the way its
panel splits the model: the **language part** (BaseLM) and the **acoustic part** (ResidualLM,
LocEnc, DiT, projections) each in its own precision. AudioVAE (the head) is always F32.

| set | BaseLM | acoustic | size |
|---|---|---|---|
| `q8-f16/` | int8 (`Int8Linear`) | F16 | 3.7 GB |
| `q8-f32/` | int8 | F32 | 5.4 GB |
| `f16-f16/` | F16 | F16 | 5.0 GB |
| `f16-f32/` | F16 | F32 | 6.7 GB |

**Why prebuilt:** the worker loads only these sets — converting the BF16 original on every
load would be slow and spike RAM (both copies in memory). The quantized sets are also faster
and lighter on VRAM (q8/f16: ~5.1 GB VRAM, ~3.3 GB RAM on an RX 9070 XT).

Each `model.pt` is a plain dict of tensors (`stan` = state dict, `bufory` = rope buffers,
`dtype`). The engine loads it with `torch.load(..., weights_only=True)` — no code runs from
the file. Made on the CPU with `pytorch/workers/voxcpm2/make_weights.py` from the repo above —
run it yourself if you prefer.

## Use

Laid out as Voicebox-on-Linux expects: `models/voxcpm-pt/prebuilt/<set>/model.pt`
(`./download-models.sh pytorch-all` fetches all four). The config and tokenizer still come from the
original repo (`models/voxcpm-pt/weights/`).

## License

Apache 2.0, as the original [openbmb/VoxCPM2](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/VoxCPM2).

# pocket-tts-onnx (upstream export)

ONNX graphs for [Kyutai's Pocket TTS](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/pocket-tts), exported with
the `export_onnx.py` script that ships with
[VolgaGerm/PocketTTS.cpp](https://github.com/VolgaGerm/PocketTTS.cpp), for use with that C++/ONNX
Runtime runtime.

Six languages: `english_2026-04`, `french_24l`, `german_24l`, `spanish_24l`, `italian_24l`,
`portuguese_24l`.

## Why this exists

The widely used [KevinAHM/pocket-tts-onnx](https://huggingface.co/KevinAHM/pocket-tts-onnx) export
predates PocketTTS.cpp's own exporter. The newer exporter changes the graph, not the weights:

* the Mimi decoder's KV cache is a **circular buffer of 250 positions** instead of 1000, matching
  the model's actual attention context — 4× less masked-out work per decode call;
* K and V caches are **separate tensors**, removing a `torch.stack` copy per step;
* KV caches are stored in **fp16** and bound as both input and output, so ONNX Runtime scatters
  in place instead of copying the cache every step.

Measured on `french_24l`, same runtime binary, same reference voice, INT8 backbone + FP32 flow and
decoder ("mixed" precision), Apple M-series, median of 5 draws over 3 sentences:

| | KevinAHM export | this export |
|---|---|---|
| RTFx | 2.03 | **2.91** |
| first-chunk latency | 723 ms | **294 ms** |
| peak RSS | 1172 MB | **842 MB** |
| Whisper WER (large-v3-turbo, fr) | 0.0 % | **0.0 %** |

Same intelligibility, ~1.4× faster, ~330 MB less resident memory.

## Contents, per language folder

| file | precision | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `flow_lm_main_int8.onnx` | INT8 | backbone; only its MatMuls are quantized, as in Kyutai's own `RECOMMENDED_CONFIG` |
| `flow_lm_flow.onnx` | FP32 | flow-matching net |
| `mimi_decoder.onnx` | FP32 | codec decoder |
| `flow_lm_flow_int8.onnx`, `mimi_decoder_int8.onnx` | INT8 | compact variants, for A/B only |
| `mimi_encoder.onnx`, `text_conditioner.onnx` | FP32 | never quantized upstream |
| `bos_before_voice.npy` | — | learned `[1,1,1024]` vector; **the runtime must prepend it** to the encoded reference voice before conditioning |
| `bundle.json` | — | runtime contract: `model_recommended_frames_after_eos`, `max_token_per_chunk`, `remove_semicolons`, `default_temperature`, plus (session 227) `pocket_tts_version`/`export_script_version` provenance — see below |
| `tokenizer.model` | — | SentencePiece |

`flow_lm_main.onnx` (FP32, 1.2 GB per language) is not published — it is only needed to validate the
INT8 quantization, which was done at export time.

### Quantizing INT8 Mimi is not free

The INT8 Mimi decoder is included for comparison, not recommended. Against the FP32 decoder on
identical latents it scores ~16.5 dB SNR, and the error is chunk-size dependent (ONNX Runtime derives
the activation scale from the chunk), correlated with the signal, and concentrated in 2–5 kHz —
audible roughness. Kyutai's own runtime never quantizes Mimi or the flow net.

## Reproducing

The upstream script is hardcoded to the 6-layer `b6369a24` English checkpoint, whose config no longer
ships with `pocket_tts` (upstream issue #12). Two changes were needed:

1. derive `FlowLMMainWrapper.NUM_LAYERS` from `len(flow_lm.transformer.layers)` — the `*_24l`
   checkpoints have 24 layers, and a hardcoded 6 silently drops 18 layers' worth of state;
2. select the config by language and let `pocket_tts` resolve the `hf://…@rev` weights.

Every export was validated against PyTorch, FP32 and INT8, with the script's own `run_validation`.

### Provenance (session 227)

Every `bundle.json` now records `pocket_tts_version` (the installed `pocket-tts` package's release
version, or `<version>+git<sha12>` when installed straight from a git ref via pip's PEP 610
`direct_url.json`) and `export_script_version` (a dated stamp bumped whenever
`tools/pockettts_export/export_onnx.py`'s export-affecting logic changes) — before this, a downloaded
bundle's staleness relative to either the upstream package or this repo's own export tooling was not
verifiable without re-running the exporter from scratch. `default_temperature` is also recorded per
language (`0.3` for English per Kyutai's own commit `d108410`, `null`/absent elsewhere — see the
runtime's `Bundle::default_temperature` for how a bundle without the key falls back unchanged).

## Licence and attribution

Weights © Kyutai, released under **CC-BY-4.0**; these are derived works (ONNX conversions) and carry
the same licence. Source model: <https://huggingface.co/kyutai/pocket-tts>. Export tooling:
VolgaGerm/PocketTTS.cpp (MIT).

# Audio8-TTS-Persian (v0.1)

A **Persian (Farsi)** fine-tune of [Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.6B](https://huggingface.co/Audio8/Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.6b), a 0.6B-parameter DualAR text-to-speech model with zero-shot voice cloning. Persian is not among the base model's supported languages; to our knowledge this is the first public Persian adaptation of Audio8.

Training code, Colab notebook and documentation: **https://github.com/ard9/Audio8-Persian-TTS**

## 🔊 Samples

| Text | Audio |
|---|---|
| سلام، امروز هوا خیلی خوب است و می‌خواهم کمی در پارک قدم بزنم. | [ft_s01.wav](samples/ft_s01.wav) |
| دیروز با دوستام رفتیم سینما، فیلمش واقعاً عالی بود! | [ft_s03.wav](samples/ft_s03.wav) |
| Voice clone (reference from a second speaker) | [clone_s01.wav](samples/clone_s01.wav) |

## Usage

The model uses Audio8's custom Transformers code (`trust_remote_code=True`). Normalize Persian text the same way as in training (digits → words, Arabic → Persian letters) with `normalize_fa` from the GitHub repo.

```python
# pip install "transformers>=4.57,<5" soundfile num2fawords
# git clone https://github.com/ard9/Audio8-Persian-TTS  (for fa_tools.normalize_fa)
import sys, torch, soundfile as sf
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoProcessor
sys.path.insert(0, "Audio8-Persian-TTS/src")
from fa_tools import normalize_fa

model_id = "ArminRahimi/Audio8-TTS-Persian"
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32

processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True, dtype=dtype).eval().to(device)

text = normalize_fa("سلام! حال شما چطور است؟")
inputs = processor(text=[text], return_tensors="pt")
# Voice cloning: add reference_audio=["ref.wav"], reference_text=[normalize_fa("exact transcript")]
inputs = {k: v.to(device) for k, v in inputs.items()}
with torch.inference_mode():
    out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024, temperature=0.8, top_p=0.95, top_k=50,
                         do_sample=True, return_dict_in_generate=True)
    wav, lengths = model.decode_audio(out.codes)
sf.write("output.wav", wav[0, : int(lengths[0])].float().cpu().numpy(), model.config.codec_sample_rate)
```

Or from the command line: `python scripts/synthesize.py --model ArminRahimi/Audio8-TTS-Persian --text "سلام" --output out.wav`.

Keep each input under ~150 characters; `scripts/synthesize.py` splits longer text into sentences automatically.

## Training details

| | |
|---|---|
| Base model | Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.6B (repo commit `07e40f5`) |
| Data | 10 of 77 Mana-TTS parts (≈ 15 h before filtering; HIGH alignment quality only, 1–20 s clips) + GPTInformal-Persian (≈ 6 h) |
| Reference conditioning | ~30% of Mana-TTS rows and 100% of GPTInformal rows trained with a same-speaker reference clip |
| Trainable parameters | Both DualAR branches (slow + fast AR), all 601M parameters |
| Optimizer | 8-bit AdamW, lr 3e-5, cosine schedule, 3% warmup, grad-norm clip 1.0 |
| Precision | fp32 master weights + autocast (bf16 on L4/A100, fp16 on T4) |
| Effective batch size | 16 (per-device batch × gradient accumulation, chosen from GPU memory) |
| Steps / epochs | 1257 / 3 |
| Hardware / time | 1× TODO GPU on Google Colab, ≈ 2.2 hours |
| Exported weights | bf16 |

## Evaluation

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Eval loss (held-out, slow + fast AR) | 9.00 (step 300) → 8.80 (step 1200) |
| CER, Whisper transcription of generated speech | not measured yet |
| MOS, native listeners | not measured yet |
| Speaker similarity (voice cloning) | not measured yet |

## Limitations

- **Small, mostly single-speaker data** (≈ 15 h Mana-TTS + ≈ 6 h GPTInformal). Voice variety and prosody are limited; cloning of unseen voices is weaker than in Audio8's supported languages.
- **Limited compute** (≈ 2.2 GPU-hours on Colab); no hyperparameter search.
- **No G2P**: unwritten short vowels, homographs and the ezafe can be mispronounced.
- Dates, abbreviations and Latin-script words are not specially normalized.
- The base model is a Preview checkpoint without Persian pre-training.
- TODO: issues you hear in the samples (e.g. mispronunciations, repetition, robotic prosody), or delete this line.

## Responsible use

This model can imitate voices. Clone a voice only with the speaker's explicit consent and disclose synthetic audio. Do not use it for impersonation, fraud or misinformation. The training data's authors prohibit using it to imitate their speakers' voices for malicious purposes.
